# The sentences

Knowing the letters is not the same as writing with them. The 1446 book, after
explaining each letter class, devoted a chapter to assembly: how letters pack
into syllable blocks.

This part is gog's version of that chapter. It moves through six groups, from
how words join into a sentence to what a reader does with the finished plot.

First the mechanics. The `+` operator layers marks in one panel, and the `*`
operator derives a compound mark from a mark and a transform. Where you write a
channel then decides whether it binds to the whole plot or to one layer.
Second, one pair of operators with two uses. `|` and `/` split one plot into a
grid of panels, and the same pair arranges separate plots on a page. Third, two
of the transforms that compute a whole picture: `flow` carries a magnitude
through its stages, and `cluster` builds the tree that puts an axis in order.

Fourth come the coordinate spaces, each a different surface to draw the plot
on. `space` needs only one more vowel, `z`, to turn a flat plot into a cube.
`polar` bends the same plane into a circle. `nest` divides a panel into
regions, each sized by its measure, that fill it with no gaps. `map` flattens
the earth onto the page, and `globe` draws it as a sphere. Each of those five
takes a sentence you can already write and draws it on a new surface. `network`
is different: its table holds relations, not positions, so a transform,
`layout`, computes where each node goes. Fifth is time, where `play` cuts the
plot into frames and shows them one after another. Last comes selection: with
`brush`, the plot's reader selects rows with the pointer, and the plot dims the
rest.

Every chapter in this part depends on one law, [Compositional
Invariance](../design-laws.qmd#law-6-compositional-invariance): a composed
expression means the same thing wherever it appears. What you build in one
chapter keeps its meaning when you use it in the next. That is what lets you
build a larger sentence from parts you learned in different chapters.
